For the Qwen and Llama models we use the pre-fitted lenses hosted by Neuronpedia ( Lin, 2023 ) (files and revision in the supplement). Its Gemma lens was fitted on the base model, so our primary Gemma lens is refitted on the instruction-tuned model from 100 WikiText sequences with a port of the reference estimator (it matches the reference code to 10 − 8 10^{-8} on a shared model); the base-model lens is a secondary readout. An entity is probed by the first token of each of its content words (at least three letters, excluding stop words such as University or Republic ); its rank is the best full-vocabulary rank among them. Tokens shared by two roles of the same item are removed, and a record left with no token for a role is dropped from statistics on that role (e.g. H1 uses 168 of Qwen3.6-27B’s 185 agents that gave in). A record is one turn of Agent 1: one item in one condition and round. The last layer is excluded from every band: it is the model’s output and identical under both lenses. 3.3. Pre-registration For each model, the prompt format, the layer band, the categories and the validation checks were chosen on the development split only and written to a pre-registration file that was committed before any of that model’s test runs and never edited. Rules changed between models, always on the new model’s development data, and every change is recorded in the files. On Qwen3.5-4B’s development split the declared threshold k = 10 k=10 selected no layers, so k = 100 k=100 was adopted before any test run (the control’s own hit@100 in the band is 0.02–0.05) and kept for all models. Two band rules were used. Rule v1 : the band is every layer (except the last) where correctly answered round-0 records read the original bridge at ≥ 0.5 \geq 0.5 ; categories need a band mean ≥ 0.5 \geq 0.5 ; an adoption check requires the peer bridge to read at least 0.3 higher when the agent is asked to assume it (hypothetical) than when it is only mentioned (mention-bridge), and the original bridge to persist when peers agree (at least half its round-0 value). Rule v2 : categories are those where the J-lens exceeds the logit lens by ≥ 0.25 \geq 0.25 in round 0; the band is every layer where, in agree dialogues, the J-lens reads ≥ 0.3 \geq 0.3 and exceeds the logit lens by ≥ 0.25 \geq 0.25 ; the adoption check becomes a ratio ( ≥ 3 × \geq 3\times ), with the same persistence check. Rule v1 was set on Qwen3.5-4B. On Qwen3.6-27B it selected only layer 62 of 64, where both lenses read the bridge equally on the development split, which would have left the lens comparison untestable; rule v2 was written on 27B’s development data before its test run, and the v1 file was kept. The change of the adoption check from a gap to a ratio relaxed it: under the absolute gap, Qwen3.6-27B’s development data would have failed (0.28 < 0.30), which the registration records. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct failed v1 (its bridge readout stayed below the threshold, and the J-lens did not beat the logit lens) and passed v2 in chat format. Rule v2 builds a J-lens advantage into the band, but it is measured on development items, whose bridges never occur in the test set, and on agents that answered alone or whose peers agreed; H4 is tested on test agents that gave in. For the v2 models H4 therefore asks whether the advantage survives giving in, not whether it exists. Gemma-4-E4B-it selected nothing under v2, because the bridge appears in both lenses at once near the output; it was registered under v1 unchanged, and its registration predicted that H4 would fail. Section 5 reports each model under the other rule where that rule selects a band. The hypotheses concern round 1 with three peers under answer pressure (H3: first- and second-hop pressure): H1 (retention): agents that gave in read their original bridge above control. H2 (registered as “implied premise”): agents that gave in read the peers’ bridge higher than agents that kept their answer in the mention condition. H3 (locus): among agents that gave in, the original bridge reads higher under second-hop than under first-hop pressure (in hindsight a check on the conditions; § 4.4 ). H4 (lens): the H1 statistic is larger under the J-lens than under the logit lens (paired within records). A hypothesis is supported if the lower end of its 95% percentile bootstrap interval ( Efron and Tibshirani, 1993 ) is above zero (1,000 resamples of records; 2,000 for the two-sample H2 and H3). Items that share a bridge are not independent; Section 5 adds intervals clustered by bridge and a correction for multiple tests. The addendum was registered after development pilots that checked only the answer format and the agree readout, and before its test runs; readout, format and categories are those of each model’s registration. For agents that gave in (answer pressure, three peers) it predicts: O1 , the original bridge reads above control under hidden; O3 , also under absent; O2 , higher under hidden than under absent (a contribution of having answered); O4 , higher under the J-lens than under the logit lens under hidden. How often agents give in Three unanimous peers asserting a wrong answer made 8% of Qwen3.5-4B’s agents give in, 25% of Gemma’s, 39% of Qwen3.6-27B’s and 90% of Llama’s (Table 1 ). Attacking the first hop, i.e. stating a wrong bridge, persuaded about as often (Qwen3.5-4B) or more; attacking the second hop while stating the correct bridge persuaded least (for Gemma only slightly: 24% vs. 25%). This ordering holds for three peers; with one or five peers it differs for some models. A single peer rarely moved an agent under answer pressure (0–10%), and more peers did not always persuade more: Gemma gave in to three peers in 25% of cases but to five in 8%. Silent dissent (H1, H4) Two kinds of comparison follow. H1 and H4 are within records: the original bridge is compared with a control entity, and the J-lens with the logit lens, for the same agents at the same position. Comparisons across conditions (Figure 2 ) are between item sets: every item appears in round 0 and in the agree condition, but held and gave in split the pressure items by outcome, and models give in more on items they are unsure of ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Differences between conditions may therefore partly reflect which items flip. Agents that gave in still represented their original bridge, and in the pre-registered layers the J-lens read it where the logit lens read little (Table 2 , Figure 2 ): 0.85, 0.22 and 0.24 under the J-lens for Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma, against 0.06, 0.00 and 0.05 under the logit lens on the same records. All three H1 and H4 tests were supported. For Llama both were formally supported but negligible (0.03). “Silent” refers to the agent’s statements and to these layers: at the output layer, identical for both lenses, the original bridge of agents that gave in is still within the top 100 tokens more often than the control (0.93, 0.82, 0.28 and 0.39), so what the logit lens misses in the band is not every trace of the bridge. Nor is it absent further down the logit lens’s ranking: without a threshold, the logit lens also ranks the original bridge above the control (for Llama only marginally), about as much as the J-lens in Qwen3.6-27B and slightly more in Gemma (§ 5 ). In these layers the J-lens brings the bridge into the top 100 tokens; it is not the only lens that ranks it above the control. Gemma gives the cleanest test of the lens comparison. Its band was chosen by rule v1, which does not look at the logit lens. Among agents that kept their answer, the two lenses read the bridge about equally (0.82 and 0.78 in round 0, 0.67 and 0.57 when peers agreed, 0.61 and 0.54 when the agent held). Among agents that gave in, on the same records, the logit lens read 0.05 and the J-lens 0.24 (H4 = 0.19 [0.14, 0.25]), although the registration had predicted H4 to be null. In the two Qwen models the J-lens reads more than the logit lens in every condition, and the logit lens reads less of the bridge in the pressure conditions (Qwen3.5-4B: 0.26 alone, 0.06 after giving in). For Qwen3.6-27B and Llama, whose bands rule v2 chose for a J-lens advantage, H4 tests whether that advantage persists in agents that gave in, not whether it exists. Retention is not uniform. For Qwen3.5-4B the readout of agents that gave in exceeds that of agents whose peers agreed (0.85 vs. 0.63); for the other models it is lower (0.22 vs. 0.50, 0.24 vs. 0.67, 0.03 vs. 0.52). Compared on the same items, giving in lowers the readout in every model (to 0.89, 0.52, 0.28 and 0.06 of the agree value); Qwen3.5-4B’s excess is consistent with which items flip: they read 0.22 [0.10, 0.31] higher than the items that held already in round 0 (exploratory, § 5 ). 4.3. The peers’ bridge (H2) Agents that gave in also represented the bridge behind the peers’ answer, which no peer stated: 0.40 for Qwen3.5-4B, 0.16 for Qwen3.6-27B and 0.21 for Gemma under the J-lens, against 0.02, 0.03 and 0.00 for agents in the mention condition, where one peer names the wrong answer and the agent keeps its own. H2 was supported for all four models (Table 2 ), negligibly for Llama. The difference is not exposure alone: agents that held under the same pressure read the peers’ bridge at 0.16, 0.03 and 0.02 (exploratory). Even a peer who names the wrong bridge outright (mention-bridge) raised its readout to only 0.18, 0.06 and 0.01, so the readout does not simply echo the context. On average, agents that gave in represent both bridges above control; whether individual agents represent both at once we did not test. Outside the capital items the peers’ answer does not determine their bridge (§3.1), so there the readout reflects association with the answer rather than inference of a premise. The registered H2 pools the categories, and split by category it rests on these: no agent of three models gave in on capital items, and the 14 agents of Qwen3.6-27B that did read the peers’ bridge only 0.02 [ − 0.10 -0.10 , 0.15] above the mention baseline (exploratory). We therefore do not claim that agents infer the premise their peers’ answer implies. 4.4. We registered it as a test of where conformity acts; it only confirms that the pressure conditions differ as intended. Table 3. Without the agent’s earlier answer Is the retained bridge read back from the agent’s own earlier answer, which stays in context, or computed again from the question? The addendum removes the answer (Table 3 ). With it hidden, agents that gave in still read their original bridge in all four models (O1), and so did agents that had never answered (O3); under hidden, the J-lens again read more than the logit lens (O4). The premise can thus be computed from the question alone. Having answered before raised the readout only for Gemma (O2); hidden and absent also differ in turn structure and wording, so O2 is not a clean test of commitment. Visible and hidden, by contrast, differ only in the text of the agent’s round-0 turn, on the same items, so they isolate whether the agent sees its earlier answer (exploratory). Seeing it anchors three models: with it hidden, Qwen3.5-4B gave in on 89% of questions instead of 8%; Llama gave in less (Table 3 ). On items where agents gave in under both, hiding the answer lowered Qwen3.5-4B’s readout by 0.44 [0.36, 0.50], so part of its main-run readout depends on the visible answer, and raised Llama’s by 0.23 [0.20, 0.27]: Llama’s near-zero retention holds only with its own answer in view (other models in the supplement). 4.6. Where in depth The J-lens advantage depends on the model (per-layer curves in the supplement). In both Qwen models the bridge becomes readable under the J-lens in intermediate layers, many layers before the logit lens reads it. In Gemma it appears only near the output, where both lenses pick it up together, as the J-lens paper observes for the last layers ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) . Llama, in its chat format, lies between: when peers agree, the J-lens reads the bridge from about layer 17 (0.52 over the band, logit lens 0.07), but in agents that gave in neither lens reads much of it before the last layers. This is unlikely to be a lens artefact: the same lens reads 0.48 in round 0 and 0.25 in agents that gave in with their earlier answer hidden, and a lens refitted on 100 WikiText sequences changes per-layer readouts by only 0.01–0.05 on the development split. Silent dissent does not require a general J-lens advantage: Gemma has little, and still shows it. 4.7.
